en.title: 40 Ways to Build a Bad Verifier
opening: Writing a good task for an agent is only half the job. The other half is giving it a verifier you can trust. Once the agent finishes, this referee looks over the task prompt, the agent environment and the deliverables, produces a score, and makes the call: pass or fail. In evaluation, that call fills one cell on a leaderboard. In training, it is the reward that drives the model's updates.

A bad call costs very different amounts in the two settings. In evaluation, a verifier that gets it wrong once leaves one number on the report card off. In training, a verifier that gets one kind of case wrong opens a gap, and the model runs straight through it. The optimizer never gives the task author the benefit of the doubt: whatever the grading leaves out, the model drops first; whatever the grading over-asks for, the model chases. By the end, the agent hasn't learned to do the work well. It has learned exactly how to play your grading script.
In principle, we ask only one thing of a verifier, so plain it sounds almost trivial:

This is the same requirement as "outcome validity" in the ABC checklist [\[1\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02825). It sounds simple, but in practice there are countless ways to break it. Worst of all, most of the time the verifier raises no error at all. It calmly produces a neatly formatted score sheet, with the problem buried inside.
The 40 rows below take these failures apart one at a time. Each row records four things: what happens, which part is at fault, what the model learns from it, and an example.
en.quote: Pass if and only if the task's goal is achieved.
terms: Criteria
What is checked, item by item, including the expected values used in judging
A rubric item, a test case
Judging method
How each criterion is judged
Programmatic check, judge model, judge model with tools
Evidence extraction
Which parts of the deliverables are handed to the judging method
File decoding, page rendering, a designated deliverable location
Aggregation
How per-criterion results become a total score and a pass verdict
Weights, must-pass criteria, pass threshold, how faults are scored
Grading environment
Where and with what the verifier runs when it grades a submission
Image and dependencies, time limits, judge-model parameters
Agent environment
What the agent can reach while doing the task; not part of the verifier, but has to be looked at together with it
Initial files and state, network, permissions

groups.name: Correct work is failed
groups.description: The goal is achieved, but the submission fails

rows.behavior: A criterion's condition can't be found in the task prompt or the provided materials, or is only half stated
rows.learning: To guess settings the task author never said out loud; when it can't guess, the score is just noise
rows.example: The prompt only says "summarize the orders by month in one table," but the criterion requires exactly 12 rows and a column named "Month." A submission that adds quarterly subtotal rows is judged not met. Hard-coded row counts, key names and table names are the usual forms

rows.behavior: Literal comparison rejects a different way of writing the same thing
rows.learning: To match one literal form
rows.example: The submission says "12.5%" and the expected value is "0.125"; the submission uses a company's short name and the expected value is its full name. Both are judged not met

rows.behavior: Evidence is collected only from one fixed location, name or file format, and isn't found anywhere else
rows.learning: To deliver in one fixed template and never change the structure
rows.example: The deliverable is saved under a different file name, or has one extra explanatory line above the table, and the verifier reports that no deliverable was found

rows.behavior: An incidental choice in the reference solution is turned into a criterion
rows.learning: To reproduce one particular solution
rows.example: The prompt asks for "a cleaned customer list." The reference solution happens to sort by name, so the criterion requires the same order

rows.behavior: The provided materials support several reasonable readings, and the criterion accepts only one
rows.learning: To gamble on a reading
rows.example: Two source tables give different addresses for the same customer, the prompt doesn't say which one wins, and the criterion accepts only one of them

rows.behavior: A programmatic check assumes an interface the prompt never specified, or uses stand-in data that is too narrow
rows.learning: To cater to how the programmatic check calls the code
rows.example: The prompt asks for "a deduplication function" without fixing argument order or return type. The programmatic check calls it with one particular order and errors out if it returns a list instead of a set

rows.behavior: The expected value itself is wrong
rows.learning: To move toward the wrong answer
rows.example: The expected value was computed by a script written when the task was authored, and the script treated tax-inclusive prices as tax-exclusive. A submission computed the way the prompt specifies is judged not met; one that makes the same mistake is judged met

rows.behavior: The judge model adds requirements of its own and checks things the criterion didn't ask
rows.learning: To do unrequested extra work as insurance
rows.example: The criterion only asks "are three recommendations given?" The judge model finds the second one not specific enough and judges it not met

rows.behavior: A minor requirement is made a must-pass criterion: violating only it leaves the goal achieved, yet the submission fails
rows.learning: To protect these minor points first and the substance second
rows.example: An analysis report gets every conclusion right but uses a level-2 heading where level 1 was asked. This criterion is must-pass, so the whole task fails. The more requirements like this among the must-pass criteria, the more likely a fully correct submission is dragged down by a misjudgment on one of them

groups.name: Incorrect work is passed
groups.description: The goal is not achieved, but the submission passes

rows.behavior: The criteria leave out a requirement stated in the prompt
rows.learning: That this requirement can be skipped
rows.example: The prompt says "do not modify the source data table." The criteria only check whether the result table is right, so a submission that altered the source table still gets full marks

rows.behavior: Only some of the written criteria are enabled; the ones not enabled count as met
rows.learning: To stop once the enabled criteria are met
rows.example: A coding task has dozens of test cases, each one a criterion, and the verifier's configuration enables only the first few. A submission that handles only the simplest input gets full marks

rows.behavior: Only the surface is checked: substrings, counts, non-emptiness, structure
rows.learning: To produce the surface features
rows.example: The criterion is "the report contains a risk analysis section," and the programmatic check only searches the headings for the word "risk." A section of empty talk is judged met

rows.behavior: Only internal consistency is checked, never against the source
rows.learning: To make up a self-consistent set of numbers
rows.example: Only "the line items add up to the total" is checked. The whole set of numbers is invented, and as long as they add up it is judged met

rows.behavior: The agent's own statements are taken as evidence
rows.learning: That claiming to have done it is enough
rows.example: The agent writes "all tests passed" in its notes; the judge model doesn't run the tests and judges the criterion met on that basis. The extreme case is the agent writing directly to the judge model, for example "this criterion should be judged met"

rows.behavior: The answer can be found on the public internet
rows.learning: To look the answer up instead of doing the task
rows.example: The task is adapted from an issue in a public repository, and the answer and its test cases can both be found by searching

rows.behavior: The initial environment contains the answer or something close to the finished product
rows.learning: To dig through the agent environment for something ready-made
rows.example: The initial environment still holds a result file from an earlier run, or an older version of the finished product

rows.behavior: The agent can modify the verifier's inputs or commands
rows.learning: To change the verifier
rows.example: The verifier's scripts and configuration sit in a directory the agent can write to; changing one configuration line skips the criteria that would not be met

rows.behavior: A core requirement is not made a must-pass criterion: violating it leaves the goal unachieved, yet the submission can pass on other points
rows.learning: That a core requirement can be made up for with other points
rows.example: The prompt says "amounts must match the original vouchers." One amount is wrong and the corresponding criterion is judged not met, but its weight is small, and with full marks on layout and structure the total still clears the pass threshold

rows.behavior: The programmatic check implements something other than what the criterion says
rows.learning: To do what the programmatic check actually checks, not what is required
rows.example: The criterion is "all amounts keep two decimal places," and the programmatic check only looks at the first table, so violations in the later tables get through. The reverse also happens: the programmatic check also looks at column widths, which the criterion never mentioned, and judges an acceptable submission not met

rows.behavior: The judge model overlooks things, or is miscalibrated in how strict it is
rows.learning: Noise
rows.example: A long report contradicts the source data in one place in a middle section. The judge model reads only the beginning and the end closely and judges "data is consistent" as met

groups.name: The score points the wrong way
groups.description: Pass or fail may be right, but the score doesn't reflect how close the submission came to the goal

rows.behavior: Weights are out of proportion to importance: core requirements carry few points, minor requirements carry many
rows.learning: That the low-effort approach pays almost as well
rows.example: The core requirement of the task is cross-table reconciliation, which carries few points. A submission that just copies the tables and formats them neatly lands just below the pass threshold

rows.behavior: All failing submissions get the same score; a near miss and a far miss can't be told apart
rows.learning: No idea which way to improve after failing
rows.example: The aggregation rule is "if any must-pass criterion is not met, the total is forced down to a fixed score below the pass threshold." Two submissions both fail, one off by a single decimal place and one barely attempted, and they get the same score

rows.behavior: Every criterion is binary; there is no partial credit
rows.learning: That half done is the same as not done
rows.example: "Reconcile all ten tables" is either met or not met. Reconciling nine and reconciling none score the same

rows.behavior: Some criteria are met by anyone and don't discriminate
rows.learning: No signal; they only dilute the total
rows.example: Criteria like "the delivery directory exists" or "the file opens" are judged met even when the initial environment is handed back untouched

rows.behavior: A single criterion's partial credit, weight and must-pass status don't fit together
rows.learning: Contradictory signals for the same performance
rows.example: A criterion allows partial credit, but it is also must-pass and counts as met only at full marks, so getting partial credit is the same as not met. Or a criterion with zero weight is must-pass

rows.behavior: One error loses points on several criteria
rows.learning: A small error is magnified; the score doesn't reflect distance from the goal
rows.example: One number is miscalculated, and the "values correct," "conclusion correct" and "chart correct" criteria are all not met

rows.behavior: Two criteria set contradictory standards for the same thing
rows.learning: They can't both be met; the model can only guess which one counts
rows.example: One criterion uses a programmatic check with a tolerance and judges a value met; a later criterion uses a judge model with literal comparison and judges the same value not met

groups.name: The result can't be trusted
groups.description: The verifier didn't run the way it claims, so the score says little

rows.behavior: A criterion is given to a judging method that can't judge it: one that needs computing or running goes to a judge model that only reads text, one that needs semantic understanding goes to a programmatic check
rows.learning: That correct work gets no credit; or that stuffing keywords earns credit
rows.example: A criterion that can only be confirmed by recomputing totals over thousands of rows is given to a judge model reading text. "Is the tone appropriate" is given to a programmatic check doing keyword matching: a submission that uses synonyms is judged not met, and empty talk stuffed with keywords is judged met

rows.behavior: The judging method doesn't get the evidence it needs
rows.learning: That this kind of requirement doesn't actually count
rows.example: It has to assess whether a chart is clear but receives only text; it has to confirm "nothing else was changed" but doesn't receive the original; long output is truncated

rows.behavior: When a programmatic check can't find what it is supposed to check, it defaults to met. This pairs with row [3](#v03): both fail to find something; there the default is not met, here it is met
rows.learning: That changing the structure dodges the programmatic check
rows.example: The programmatic check finds a column by its header name. The submission words the header differently, the programmatic check can't find it and returns no verdict, and the criterion is treated as met

rows.behavior: What is read is a stale value or the wrong object
rows.learning: To change the surface without changing the result
rows.example: A formula in a spreadsheet was changed but not recalculated, and the programmatic check reads the cached old result; or it reads a different table with the same name

rows.behavior: Regrading the same submission changes the verdict
rows.learning: Noise
rows.example: The same submission is graded twice; the "argument is well supported" criterion is judged met the first time and not met the second, and the total crosses the pass threshold

rows.behavior: A subjective criterion has no yardstick
rows.learning: Noise
rows.example: The criterion only says "clearly expressed" without saying what counts as clear, and the judge model reads it differently on two runs

rows.behavior: The grading itself broke, but it is counted as the submission failing and scored zero
rows.learning: The penalty isn't for the submission
rows.example: A dependency fails to install during grading, the programmatic checks never run, and the result is recorded as zero

rows.behavior: The submission failed, but it is counted as a grading fault and gets no score
rows.learning: That failure doesn't count
rows.example: The submission breaks the agent environment so the programmatic checks can't start; it is filed as a "grading fault" and then retried or dropped

rows.behavior: The score the verifier reports doesn't match what it actually ran
rows.learning: The score has nothing to do with the submission
rows.example: Two forms: grading didn't finish but a score is issued as usual, or it finished and the result was then voided by a later step. For example, the judge model's output is truncated and the half that parses is scored as usual; some programmatic checks didn't run and the score is issued as if all were met; a criterion is marked as judged by a programmatic check, but that check is empty and a judge model judges it instead, with nothing in the result to show it; grading is complete and a timeout in a cleanup step voids the result

rows.behavior: Grading has to download things over the network at run time: if the download fails nothing can be graded, and if the downloaded version changes the result changes
rows.learning: No direct effect on the model, but the result depends on the network
rows.example: Dependencies are installed on the spot during grading, and a failed download means this run can't be graded; a slow download uses up the grading time limit

rows.behavior: The grading environment itself is incomplete
rows.learning: No direct effect on the model, but no verdict comes out
rows.example: The grading environment lacks build dependencies or can't find the toolchain; the programmatic check itself raises an error

rows.behavior: Grading is tied to one particular judge model or to its output budget
rows.learning: No direct effect on the model, but grading breaks with a different judge model
rows.example: The call to the judge model uses a parameter only one model supports; the judge model thinks for too long, uses up its output budget and gives no verdict

rows.behavior: The score can't be re-verified: the deliverables and grading dependencies weren't pinned, so regrading later is impossible or gives a different result
rows.learning: No direct effect on the model, but the score can't be checked
rows.example: Deliverables aren't archived; grading dependencies aren't version-pinned, and regrading some time later gives a different result

en.discussionTitle: Looking back: only two kinds of error
discussionBefore: The root requirement is an "if and only if," so a verifier can only go wrong in two ways. The goal is achieved but the submission fails: a false fail. The goal is not achieved but the submission passes: a false pass.
comparison: The grading is narrower than the goal
The grading is broader than the goal
How it gets narrower or broader

The goal allows many ways of doing it, but the grading accepts only one: one wording (row [2](#v02)), one location (row [3](#v03)), the reference solution's approach (row [4](#v04)), one reading (row [5](#v05)), one interface (row [6](#v06)). Or it adds conditions beyond the goal (rows [1](#v01), [8](#v08), [9](#v09))

It checks only part of the goal (rows [10](#v10), [11](#v11), [18](#v18), [20](#v20)). It checks a stand-in that is easier to satisfy than the goal (rows [12](#v12), [13](#v13), [14](#v14), [24](#v24)). Or the checks get bypassed (rows [15](#v15), [16](#v16), [17](#v17), [30](#v30))
To narrow: guess the one form the grading accepts, and never try a different approach
To cut corners: skip whatever isn't checked, and fake whatever can be faked
discussionAfter: The last two groups are the same two errors in different places. Group 3 gets the size of the score wrong. A near miss and a barely attempted submission get the same score (rows [22](#v22){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v22-0}, [23](#v23){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v23-0}): a false fail against the near miss. Skipping the core still lands close to passing (row [21](#v21){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v21-0}): a false pass for the low-effort submission. In group 4 you can't even tell which way it went wrong. Regrading the same submission changes the verdict (row [32](#v32){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v32-0}). A grading fault counted as the submission failing is a false fail (row [34](#v34){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v34-0}); a submission failure counted as a grading fault is a false pass (row [35](#v35){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v35-0}).

**False fails and false passes are not two ends of one axis.** One comes from grading that is narrower than the goal, the other from grading that is broader, and both can show up on different criteria of the same verifier. Make the whole verifier stricter, and false passes go down while false fails go up; make it looser, and the reverse happens. To reduce both at once, what needs adjusting is not strictness but whether what the grading accepts matches the goal. Switching the judging method is no different: moving a criterion from a judge model to a programmatic check changes where the false fails and false passes show up. It doesn't make them go away.

**The two errors teach the model bad habits in different ways.** When people talk about reward hacking, they mean false passes: the model learns to cut corners, which at least shows in the results. False fails are quieter. The model isn't cheating; it just does things in a narrower and narrower way, looking more and more like the one answer the grading accepts.
notes: The examples in the tables are constructed for illustration and do not come from real tasks.
This post reflects only the author's personal views, not those of the author's team or company.

zh.title: 把 verifier 做坏的 40 种办法
opening: 给 agent 出了一道好题，事情其实只做了一半——另一半，是给它配一个靠谱的 verifier。作答一结束，这个裁判要翻看题面、作答环境和交付物，给出一个分数，再拍板“过”还是“不过”。放在评测里，它决定榜单上的一格；放到训练里，它就是驱动模型更新的 reward。
同样是裁判吹偏哨，这两处的代价完全不在一个量级。评测里 verifier 错一次，最多是成绩单上某个数字不准；训练里 verifier 只要错一类，模型就会顺着这个口子一路狂奔。优化器从不体谅出题人的本意：评分漏掉什么，模型就第一时间省掉什么；评分多要什么，模型就拼命迎合什么。练到最后，agent 没学会怎么把活干好，倒先学会了怎么精准拿捏你的评分脚本。
按理说，我们对 verifier 只有一条根本要求，朴素得近乎废话：
这和 ABC 检查清单 [\[1\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02825) 里的“结果有效性”是同一回事。听起来简单明了，真落到工程里却有无数种破法——最麻烦的是，大多数时候 verifier 根本不会报错，照样稳稳当当地吐出一张格式工整的分数表，把坑藏得严严实实。
下面这 40 条，把这些坑逐一拆开，每一条记下四件事：出了什么现象、坏在哪个部分、模型会顺着学到什么，外加一个例子。
zh.quote: 通过，当且仅当题目的目的达成了。
terms: 评分项
逐条查什么，含判定时用到的期望值
一条评分标准、一个测试用例
判定器
每个评分项怎么判
程序检查、评判模型、带工具的评判模型
证据抽取
把交付物里的哪些内容交给判定器
文件解码、页面渲染、指定交付物位置
聚合规则
各评分项的结果怎么变成总分和通过结论
权重、必过项、通过线、故障怎么记分
评分环境
verifier 给作答打分时在哪跑、用什么跑
镜像和依赖、时限、评判模型的参数
作答环境
作答方做题时能接触到的东西，不属于 verifier，但要和它一起看
初始文件和状态、网络、权限

rows.behavior: 评分项的条件在题面和公开材料里找不到，或只露了一半
rows.learning: 猜出题人没说出口的设定；猜不到时分数只是噪声
rows.example: 题面只说“把订单按月汇总成一张表”，评分项却要求恰好 12 行、列名必须叫“月份”。加了季度小计行的作答被判不满足。常见的是写死的条数、键名、表名

rows.behavior: 按字面比对，拒掉意思相同的另一种写法
rows.learning: 对齐某一种字面形态
rows.example: 作答写“12.5%”，期望值是“0.125”；作答写公司简称，期望值是全称。都被判不满足

rows.behavior: 只到一个固定位置、固定名称或固定文件形态去取证，换了就找不到
rows.learning: 照固定模板交付，不敢换结构
rows.example: 交付物存成了另一个文件名，或者在表前多加了一行说明，verifier 报告找不到交付物

rows.behavior: 参考答案里碰巧的做法被写成评分项
rows.learning: 复现某一份答案的做法
rows.example: 题面要“清洗后的客户名单”。参考答案碰巧按姓名排序，评分项就要求同样的顺序

rows.behavior: 公开材料支持多种合理口径，评分项只认其中一种
rows.learning: 赌口径
rows.example: 两份原始表里同一客户的地址不一样，题面没说以哪份为准，评分项只认其中一份

rows.behavior: 程序检查假定了题面没声明的接口，或用的替身数据太窄
rows.learning: 迎合程序检查的调用方式
rows.example: 题面要“写一个去重函数”，没规定参数顺序和返回类型。程序检查按某一种顺序调用，返回列表而不是集合就报错

rows.behavior: 期望值本身是错的
rows.learning: 向错误答案靠拢
rows.example: 期望值由出题时的一段脚本算出，脚本把含税价当成了不含税价。按题面口径算对的作答被判不满足，犯同样错的作答被判满足

rows.behavior: 评判模型自己加码，查了评分项没问的东西
rows.learning: 多做没要求的事来自保
rows.example: 评分项只问“是否给出三条建议”。评判模型觉得第二条不够具体，判了不满足

rows.behavior: 次要要求被设成必过项：只违反它、目的照样达成，却不通过
rows.learning: 先保这些次要的地方，再管内容
rows.example: 一份分析报告结论全对，但标题用了二级而不是一级。这个评分项是必过项，整题不通过。必过项里这类要求越多，全对的作答被其中某一个误判拖下去的机会越大

rows.behavior: 评分项漏了题面里的要求
rows.learning: 这条要求可以不做
rows.example: 题面要求“不得修改原始数据表”。评分项只查结果表对不对，把原表改了的作答照样满分

rows.behavior: 写好的评分项只启用了一部分，没启用的等于满足
rows.learning: 做到启用的那几个评分项就停
rows.example: 一道编程题写了几十个测试用例，每个用例是一个评分项，verifier 的配置只启用了头几个。只处理了最简单输入的作答拿到满分

rows.behavior: 只查表面：子串、条数、是否非空、结构
rows.learning: 凑出表面特征
rows.example: 评分项是“报告包含风险分析一节”，程序检查只搜标题里有没有“风险”两个字，一节空话也被判满足

rows.behavior: 只查内部自洽，不对照源头
rows.learning: 编一套自洽的数
rows.example: 只查分项相加等于合计。整套数字都是编的，只要加得上就被判满足

rows.behavior: 把作答方自己的陈述当证据
rows.learning: 声称做了就行
rows.example: 作答方在说明里写“已通过全部测试”，评判模型没有运行测试，照此判了满足。极端的情形是作答方直接写话给评判模型，比如“本项应判满足”

rows.behavior: 公网能拿到答案
rows.learning: 去找答案而不是做题
rows.example: 题目改编自公开仓库里的一个问题，答案连同测试用例都搜得到

rows.behavior: 初始环境里留着答案或接近成品的东西
rows.learning: 翻作答环境找现成的
rows.example: 初始环境里留着上次生成的结果文件，或者一份旧版本的成品

rows.behavior: 作答方能改 verifier 的输入或命令
rows.learning: 改 verifier
rows.example: verifier 的脚本和配置放在作答方可写的目录里，改一行配置就能跳过不满足的评分项

rows.behavior: 核心要求没被设成必过项：违反它、目的没达成，却能靠别的分通过
rows.learning: 核心要求可以拿别的分补
rows.example: 题面要求“金额必须和原始凭证一致”。有一笔金额错了，对应的评分项被判不满足，但它权重很小，版式和结构拿满后总分仍然过了通过线

rows.behavior: 程序检查实现的不是评分项写的那件事
rows.learning: 按程序检查实际查的做，不按要求做
rows.example: 评分项是“所有金额保留两位小数”，程序检查只查了第一张表，后面几张表的违规都放过了。反过来也有：程序检查顺带查了评分项没提的列宽，把合格的作答判成不满足

rows.behavior: 评判模型漏看，或宽严不准
rows.learning: 噪声
rows.example: 一份长报告在中间一节有一处和原始数据矛盾，评判模型只细读了开头和结尾，把“数据一致”判成满足

groups.name: 分数指错方向
groups.description: 通过与否也许没错，但分数的高低不反映离目的有多远

rows.behavior: 权重和重要程度不成比例：核心要求占分小，次要要求占分大
rows.learning: 省事做法几乎一样划算
rows.example: 题目的核心要求是跨表核对，占分很小。只把表抄一遍、排好版的作答离通过线只差一点

rows.behavior: 不通过的作答都是同一个分，差一点和差很多分不开
rows.learning: 没通过时不知道往哪改
rows.example: 聚合规则是“任何一个必过项不满足，总分就压到通过线下的一个固定分”。两份作答都没通过，一份只差一个小数位，一份几乎没做，得分一样

rows.behavior: 评分项全是二值，没有部分分
rows.learning: 做到一半和没做一样
rows.example: “完成全部十张表的核对”只有满足和不满足。核对了九张的和一张没做的同分

rows.behavior: 有些评分项谁都能满足，不提供区分
rows.learning: 没有信号，只稀释总分
rows.example: “交付目录存在”“文件能打开”这类评分项，连原样交回初始环境也被判满足

rows.behavior: 同一个评分项的部分分、权重和必过要求对不上
rows.learning: 同一表现得到互相矛盾的信号
rows.example: 某个评分项允许给部分分，可它又是必过项、要拿满分才算满足，拿到部分分就等于不满足。又如一个权重为零的评分项却是必过项

rows.behavior: 同一个错误在多个评分项上扣分
rows.learning: 小错被放大，分数不反映离目的多远
rows.example: 一个数字算错，“数值正确”“结论正确”“图表正确”三个评分项一起不满足

rows.behavior: 两个评分项对同一件事的标准互相矛盾
rows.learning: 没法同时满足，只能猜哪一个算数
rows.example: 一个评分项由程序检查按容差判某个数值满足，后面一个评分项由评判模型按字面比对，判同一个数值不满足

groups.name: 结论不可信
groups.description: verifier 没有按它声称的方式跑完，分数说明不了什么

rows.behavior: 评分项交给了判不了它的判定器：要算、要跑的给了只读文本的评判模型，要理解语义的给了程序检查
rows.learning: 做对了也拿不到分；或者堆关键词就能拿分
rows.example: 要重算上千行合计才能确认的评分项，让评判模型读文本判。“语气是否得体”交给程序检查做关键词匹配，用了同义词的被判不满足，堆了关键词的空话被判满足

rows.behavior: 判定器拿不到需要的证据
rows.learning: 这类要求实际不计分
rows.example: 要看图表是否清晰，判定器只拿到文字；要核“其余部分没改动”，判定器拿不到原稿；长输出被截断

rows.behavior: 程序检查找不到要查的东西时，默认算满足。它和第 [3](#v03) 条是一对：同样是找不到，那边默认不满足，这边默认满足
rows.learning: 换个结构就躲过程序检查
rows.example: 程序检查按表头名找列。作答把表头换了个说法，程序检查找不到就不出结论，这个评分项当作满足

rows.behavior: 读到的是旧值或错的对象
rows.learning: 改表面不改结果
rows.example: 表格里公式改了没重算，程序检查读到的是缓存的旧结果；或者读到了同名的另一张表

rows.behavior: 同一份作答重评，结论改变
rows.learning: 噪声
rows.example: 同一份作答评两次，“论证充分”这个评分项第一次判满足，第二次判不满足，总分正好跨过通过线

rows.behavior: 主观的评分项没有标尺
rows.learning: 噪声
rows.example: 评分项只写“表达清晰”，没说什么算清晰，评判模型两次各有各的理解

rows.behavior: 评分自己出了故障，却算成作答失败，记零分
rows.learning: 被罚的不是作答
rows.example: 评分时依赖装不上，程序检查根本没跑，结果记成零分

rows.behavior: 作答失败，却算成评分故障，不出分
rows.learning: 失败不被计入
rows.example: 作答把作答环境改坏，程序检查起不来，被归成“评分故障”后重试或剔除

rows.behavior: verifier 给出的分数和它实际跑的情况对不上
rows.learning: 分数和作答无关
rows.example: 有两种：评分没跑完却照常出分，或跑完了结果却被后续步骤作废。比如评判模型的输出被截断，解析出半截结果照常计分；一部分程序检查没执行，按全部满足出分；评分项标着由程序检查判，那段程序检查其实是空的，改由评判模型判，结果里看不出来；评分已完成，收尾步骤超时把结果作废

rows.behavior: 评分要现场联网下载：下载失败就评不了，下到的版本变了结果就变
rows.learning: 不直接影响模型，但结果取决于网络
rows.example: 评分时现场安装依赖，下载失败这次就评不了；下载慢的时候把评分时限耗尽

rows.behavior: 评分环境自身不完整
rows.learning: 不直接影响模型，但出不了结论
rows.example: 评分环境缺编译依赖、找不到工具链；程序检查自己报错

rows.behavior: 绑定某个评判模型或它的输出额度
rows.learning: 不直接影响模型，但换个评判模型就评不了
rows.example: 调用评判模型时用了只有一种模型支持的参数；评判模型思考太长，把输出额度用完，没给出结论

rows.behavior: 分数没法复核：交付物和评分依赖没固定下来，事后重评不了，或重评结果不同
rows.learning: 不直接影响模型，但分数无法复核
rows.example: 交付物没归档；评分依赖没固定版本，过一阵再评结果不同

zh.discussionTitle: 回头看这 40 条：只有两种错
discussionBefore: 根本要求是“当且仅当”，所以 verifier 只会以两种方式出错：目的达成了，却判不通过，这是错杀；目的没达成，却判通过，这是放水。
comparison: 目的允许多种做法，评分只认一种：一种写法（第 [2](#v02) 条）、一个位置（第 [3](#v03) 条）、参考答案的做法（第 [4](#v04) 条）、一种口径（第 [5](#v05) 条）、一种接口（第 [6](#v06) 条）；或者在目的之外多加了条件（第 [1](#v01)、[8](#v08)、[9](#v09) 条）
收窄：猜评分认的那一种，不敢换做法
偷工：评分不查的就不做，能凑出来的就不真做
discussionAfter: 后两组也是这两种错，只是换了地方。第三组错在分数的高低上：差一点的和几乎没做的同分（第 [22](#v22){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v22-0}、[23](#v23){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v23-0} 条），是对差一点那份的错杀；不碰核心也能拿到接近通过的分（第 [21](#v21){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v21-0} 条），是对省事那份的放水。第四组是连错往哪边都不知道：同一份作答重评，结论会变（第 [32](#v32){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v32-0} 条）；评分自己的故障算成作答失败是错杀（第 [34](#v34){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v34-0} 条），作答失败算成评分故障是放水（第 [35](#v35){:#ve-ref-argument-1-v35-0} 条）。
**错杀和放水不在一根轴上。** 一个来自评分比目的窄，一个来自评分比目的宽，它们可以同时出现在同一套 verifier 的不同评分项上。所以整体调严，放水少了，错杀就多了；整体调松，反过来。要两种错一起少，调的不是严和松，而是评分认的东西和目的对不对得上。换判定器也是一样：把一个评分项从评判模型换给程序检查，换掉的是错杀和放水各出在哪里，不是让它们消失。
**两种错教坏模型的方式不同。** 人们谈 reward hacking，说的是放水：模型学会偷工，至少在结果上还看得出来。错杀更安静：模型没有作弊，只是做法越来越窄，越来越像评分认的那一份答案。
notes: 表里的例子都是为说明而构造的，不来自真实题目。
本文只代表作者个人观点，不代表作者所在的团队或公司。

labels.scheme: 一套 verifier 由五个部分组成，再加上作答环境。
